items.title: Lagging behind
items.description: THE IMF’s latest World Economic Outlook projects Pakistan’s economy to grow by 3.5pc in the current fiscal year, while average inflation climbs to 9.9pc. The current account is expected to slip into a deficit of 1pc of GDP. This forecast points to an economy that remains vulnerable despite recent gains in macroeconomic stability. The economy expanded by 3.6pc last year. Further slowdown matters for a country with a rapidly increasing population, entrenched poverty, and high unemployment. Growth at this pace will hardly raise incomes meaningfully or absorb new entrants into the labour market. Inflation poses another challenge. After easing to 7.1pc last year, it is forecast to rise sharply, leading to fears of further erosion of purchasing power. For families already squeezed by high energy costs, taxes, and essential expenses, renewed price pressures will undermine any benefits from economic stabilisation. The projected current account deficit signals renewed pressure on foreign exchange earnings. Higher oil prices and shipping disruptions make imports more expensive. Unless exports grow faster and are more diversified, stronger domestic demand could again widen the external gap. The IMF expects unemployment to decline to 6.5pc in FY27 from 6.9pc the previous year. But, in the absence of stronger growth, which can create a sufficient number of jobs, that is hardly of any comfort. It does not establish whether new jobs will be productive, secure or adequately paid. Nor does it show whether employment is expanding fast enough to keep pace with the working-age population. The South Asia region is forecast to grow by 6.4pc in 2026. Pakistan’s 3.5pc projection places it far below the regional average, highlighting our failure to build a sustained growth engine. The global picture is also distressing. The IMF forecasts global growth of 3.1pc in 2026, rising to 3.4pc in 2027. Investment in AI is supporting activity in some economies. Others face higher energy costs, trade disruptions, and tighter financial conditions. Growth is also becoming increasingly uneven. We must prepare for these pressures rather than assume that stabilisation will deliver prosperity. The immediate task is to contain inflation and protect vulnerable households without reviving unsustainable subsidies or excessive demand. For that, the government must shift resources towards productive investment, improve the competitiveness of industry, broaden the tax base and expand export capacity. Better education, skills, and employment opportunities are equally important. These changes require consistent policies, not another short-lived cycle of incentives and concessions. The IMF projections expose the cost of postponing structural reform. An economy growing at 3.5pc, with inflation approaching double digits and a weakening external balance, remains vulnerable to the next shock. Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

items.title: Afghan Taliban’s ‘cheap but deadly’ drone campaign
items.description: • Islamabad reported 23 drone incursions in September alone • Afghan drones run on 55cc engines commercially available online; low-cost ‘suicide weapons’ can carry up to 1kg explosives, posing hard-to-detect threat to infrastructure • Experts warn UAVs can inflict ‘heavy psychological damage’ BUILDING an air force no longer requires a proper defence budget, it just takes a 3D printer, open-source autopilot software and an internet connection. Over the skies of Pakistan, the Afghan Taliban are proving just how low the barrier to aerial warfare has fallen. In a conflict where one side commands modern fighter jets and aerial superiority, the other is fighting back with makeshift quadcopters and two-metre fixed-wing drones powered by online-bought piston engines. These unmanned aircraft are built to haunt the skies and fray the nerves of the other side, according to a report by France’s state-owned media outlet France24. On September 23, Pakistan’s military forces shot down at least eight fixed-wing drones in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa fewer than 1,000 metres from the Afghan border, marking the latest cross-border unmanned aerial assault targeting Pakistan. Five days later, on Sept 28, the Foreign Ministry issued a diplomatic protest note to the Taliban over what it called “provocative incursions”, reporting that 23 drones had entered Pakistani airspace from Afghanistan since the beginning of September. The Taliban have increasingly relied on unmanned aircraft since open conflict erupted between the two neighbours in February. Psychological warfare An examination by France24 of photographs and videos showing drones intercepted by the Pakistan Army revealed that Taliban’s suicide aircraft appear to run on DLE55 engines. Those 55cc single-piston engines are readily available for commercial purchase online. Unmanned aerial vehicle expert Mark Grozel told France24 that these drones measure approximately two metres across and carry between half a kilogram and one kilogram of explosives. Because they fly slowly and at low altitudes, they offer limited military effectiveness and are simple to shoot down once spotted, though detecting them remains a challenge, Grozel said. While a foreign government could be supplying the aircraft, Grozel noted that building a homemade fixed-wing drone is no longer difficult. Autopilot trajectory software is widely accessible, engines and batteries are sold on the e-commerce platform Alibaba, and airframes that are cheap to make can be constructed using 3D printers, polystyrene or balsa wood, according to Grozel. Despite relying on rudimentary radio navigation, basic engines and small payloads, the unmanned aircraft inflict heavy psychological damage. “They allow you to tell your adversary: ‘I can threaten your infrastructure at any moment’. If one hits a school or a fuel facility, the consequences could be catastrophic. Their main power is their psychological impact,” Grozel said. Open conflict Islamabad and Kabul saw their relationship collapse roughly eight months ago when Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Mohammad Asif publicly stated that “relations with the Taliban had deteriorated into an ‘open war’.” Tensions boiled over after Pakistan launched airstrikes inside Afghanistan targeting the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). The TTP is an internationally designated terrorist organisation. Pakistan accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring and aiding the TTP, which has waged an insurgency inside Pakistan for nearly 20 years. Possessing aerial superiority, Pakistan has struck suspected TTP hideouts deep within Afghan territory. The Afghan Taliban have answered such strikes with ground assaults and drone attacks. Throughout 2025, routine border fighting reportedly claimed around 4,000 lives, and on Sept 18, 2026, a TTP suicide car bombing at a mosque in the Pakistani border city of Kohat killed 21 people. Mukhtar Wafaei, an Afghan affairs specialist and expert on the Taliban, told France24 that the alliance between the two groups dates back to the 1980s Soviet-Afghan War, when religious schools in Pakistan sent Afghan and Pakistani fighters to wage “jihad” against Soviet troops. After the US-led invasion toppled the first Taliban regime following the Sept 11, 2001, attacks, Taliban fighters fled into Pakistan’s border areas, including Balochistan, Waziristan and KP. Shared roots According to France24, there is a very deep ideological relationship between the Afghan Taliban and the TTP, rooted in their shared background of attending religious schools in Pakistan. They share the same ideology, come from the same religious tradition and follow the same teachings. They can no longer be separated. They are effectively one group. A few months after the Afghan Taliban returned to power, the TTP leader stated very clearly in Pashto that TTP and the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, meaning the Afghan Taliban, were one group. He said: “We are not two groups. We are one group, following one programme, one ideology and one method.” This is particularly revealing because the TTP leader himself explicitly described the two movements as one. Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

items.title: Government to introduce integrated basic education model schools from 2027 – Haruna Iddrisu
items.description: The Education Minister, Haruna Iddrisu, has announced the government’s intention to introduce integrated basic education model schools from 2027. He explained that the model would include structured education from kindergarten to junior high school, providing a comprehensive one-stop centre for basic education. He announced this at the 64th Annual National Conference of the Conference of Heads of Assisted Secondary Schools (CHASS) in Ho, in the Volta Region. He said the initiative aims to address the country’s infrastructure deficit, with reports by the Auditor General indicating that about 3 million pupils in 10,730 schools across 13 regions lack classrooms, forcing pupils to learn in unfavourable conditions. “For literacy to succeed, we have to realign investment and spending to foundational learning and basic education. I’m happy to know that from 2020, there will be only one new model of an integrated basic school built everywhere in Ghana.” “That integrated model basic school will have a kindergarten, a primary school block, a junior school block, a changing room, ICT, STEM, laboratory, and water processing facilities housed in the same facility across Ghana”, he said. He indicated that construction of the integrated basic education model schools would commence across the country next, as the President has already given executive approval for the project The President of the Conference of Heads of Assisted Secondary Schools, Rev. Fr. Stephen Owusu Sekyere, alluded to the lack of enough furniture, infrastructure and vehicles in schools across the country. “We call on government to roll out an emergency intervention to resolve this enduring problem. We also appeal to government to complete the several stalled GETFund projects in schools”, he appealed. He said that the continuous delay in the release of operational funds for the schools has made administration of the school “stressful”. He urged the government to adopt a predictable funding mechanism to ensure the timely release of funds and also clear perishable and recurrent arrears from 2021 to 2025. “Outstanding balances spanning from 2021 to 2024 remain unpaid and require urgent settlement to enable schools to clear their longstanding indebtedness to benevolent creditors”, he said.

items.title: Two ships sink near Hormuz after being hit by projectiles
items.description: LONDON: A container ship and a dry bulk carrier both sank near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday. Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month. The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride, a small container vessel with a capacity of 2,824 20-foot equivalent units (TEU), sank while sailing through the strait, according to maritime security sources. “GFS PRIDE sustained damage and a fire on board, and has since sunk. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated. No injuries have been reported,” the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) said in a statement on Wednesday, adding that the vessel had been sailing through the strait on Tuesday. In a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, weeks after being struck by a projectile on September 23, data from UN shipping agency the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) showed on Wednesday. One crew member was killed, the rest of the crew evacuated straight after the strike, maritime sources said. Its UAE-based manager Peonies Shipmanagement FZE could not be immediately reached for comment. The GFS Pride and Cape Dao are the second and third vessels to have sunk since the US-Iran war began on Feb 28, according to an analysis of IMO casualty data. “MPA is deeply concerned about the continued attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz,” the Singapore authority said. “Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law.” “The latest incidents reinforce the continuing threat to commercial shipping transiting the Strait of Hormuz,” maritime risk management company MARISKS said on Wednesday. “The threat is not confined to tankers, with container vessels and bulk carriers also sustaining serious damage.” Iran is increasingly deploying new tactics against vessels transiting the strait as it seeks to keep oil prices elevated and influence US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters. While Iran and the US have focused their attacks on tankers, cargo and container vessels have also been attacked, immobilised or sunk. Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

items.title: Russell Brand was a ‘sexual predator’, prosecution alleges as rape trial begins
items.description: Russell Brand was described as “ruthless” and a “sexual predator” by the prosecution at the start of his trial for rape and sexual assault on Wednesday. The 51-year-old actor and comedian faces three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges. Riel Karmy-Jones KC, for the prosecution, told Southwark Crown Court in London the women “did not know each other”, “have never met each other” and “came forward independently of each other”. Russell Brand pictured in the dock on Wednesday in a court sketch The barrister said: “The circumstances of the offending were as wide and as varied as the defendant’s career.” She said that “regardless of who the women were and what they said or did, Brand was not deterred”. “His desire, strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious,” she told the court. The prosecutor told jurors that Brand would be “nice when he wanted to be, funny – undoubtedly – charming, likeable even, when he wanted something in return”. But she said he would also be “demanding, entitled, a flirt with a huge sexual appetite – childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met”. The prosecutor said Brand would “appear indifferent, normal and untroubled by what had just occurred” after the encounters. She added that “sometimes he would leave promptly after the incident, sometimes making an excuse to get away, or sometimes simply continuing as though nothing wrong had happened”. Brand’s wife Laura joined him at court on Wednesday On Wednesday, the jury heard details of the alleged offences. The first complainant says she met Brand before he was famous in 1999, the jury was told. She had attended the Labour Party conference and went to a fringe event where she spoke to Brand. He later allegedly raped her. The prosecution said when Brand was questioned by police about this allegation of rape, “he said if it happened, he didn’t remember the incident”. He added that he did not remember the first complainant’s name and that he “had never engaged in non-consensual activity”. The second complainant worked for MTV at the time when she says Brand indecently assaulted her. She said Brand asked her where the toilets were and the woman offered to show him. When they reached the toilets, prosecutors say, Brand asked the woman to “come in” before grabbing her forearm. She resisted by struggling and pulling back. He had what she described as a desperate, wild-eyed look on his face, as he said: “Please please come in – oh go on.” The third complainant says Brand orally raped her in a toilet after meeting her at a party in 2004. Within a minute of meeting, in the middle of a conversation, he lurched forward and grabbed her breasts and squeezed them with both hands, the jury was told. The prosecution said the woman remembered he had a “big, weird grin” on his face as he did so, then grabbed her arm and pulled her towards the toilets. The same woman said that as they were driving to another venue, Brand exposed himself, the court heard. “He said, ‘Come on, come on, suck it’ – to which she just said, ‘No no’,” the prosecution added. “He simply laughed but appeared to accept her refusal.” The fourth complainant says Brand pushed her up against a wall at Capital Radio in 2004 or 2005 and kissed her “sloppily and aggressively”, and “grabbed her body, at her breasts, sides and buttocks, aggressively”. She was able to push him away and he “just sniggered, like it was a joke”, the prosecutor said. The jury then heard how the fifth complainant says she met Brand when he was performing at the Hammersmith Apollo in London in 2009. The prosecution said their encounter began with consensual activity, but that he raped her anally on a later occasion. The jury heard how the woman “spent months and years blaming herself”, becoming anxious and unwell. They were told Brand texted the woman after seeing her at an event the following summer, saying: “I wanna push you further.” She is said to have replied: “I think you pushed me far enough – you treated me like an animal.” He allegedly replied: “I’m sorry.” The sixth complainant – who has accused Brand of sexual assault – says he demanded a massage when she was on a work assignment in 2009. He “fell to his knees and placed his head directly into her groin area”, the prosecution said. After the accounts of the final two women were heard, the prosecutor said Brand told police in 2023 “he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity, and that any accounts had been reinvented or imagined after a defamatory documentary and subsequent press reporting”. On Wednesday afternoon, Brand’s former flatmate Mark Pinheiro was the first witness to give evidence. Pinheiro told jurors that Brand had told him he may have gone a “bit too far” with a woman when visiting the Labour Party conference in 1999. “He said that things got a little bit heated and a little bit out of hand, and he thinks that maybe he did go a little bit too far. “Those were his words – ‘I think I may have gone a bit too far’.” Pinheiro was pressed under cross-examination about whether he accurately remembered the comment, but he told the court he was sure Brand had said “things may have gone a little bit too far” or “I may have taken things a little too far”. The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks. Brand was accompanied by his wife Laura to the court on Wednesday. He rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother’s Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music. He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States.

items.title: World Bank sees ‘moderate’ progress in Pakistan's tax reforms
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The World Bank on Wednesday rated its two loan programmes in Pakistan, worth around $670 million, as ‘moderately satisfactory’ with ‘substantial risk’. The programmes are intended to support macroeconomic stability, improve service delivery and increase the tax-to-GDP ratio to 15pc in five years. In its public disclosure, the Washington-based lending agency rated the overall implementation of the $700 million financing for the Pakistan Public Resources for Inclusive Development — Multiphase Programmatic Approach (PRID-MPA) as ‘moderately satisfactory’. It assigned a substantial risk rating to the loan, which became effective on June 19, 2025. One of the programme’s key objectives is to increase Pakistan’s tax-to-GDP ratio from 12.3pc in June 2025 to 15pc by June 2030. The rating is based on high political and governance risk, and moderate to substantial risks across macroeconomic, sector strategies and policies, institutional capacity, fiduciary, and environmental and social standards. Overall risks have been described as ‘substantial’. The MPA operation became effective on May 14, and an advance disbursement of $164.52 million was made on June 29. Despite these risks, the bank noted strong progress across most of the disbursement-linked indicators, “reflecting continued momentum in the reform programme”. It said the government was operationalising the technical assistance component and related implementation arrangements, following refinements to project activities and cost allocations. Washington-based lender flags substantial risks to $670 million programmes The two sides — the government and the World Bank — are now working closely to advance preparatory activities and mitigate the impact of delays in approval timelines on fulfilment of effectiveness conditions and reform implementation. The World Bank has reported to the government for correction the delays on account of the constitution of the governing council of the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics and the appointment of the chief statistician — a key lapse in programme conditions. Under this, the chief statistician position should not remain vacant during the programme implementation, and an existing government official may not be formally delegated the role of chief statistician. The condition has been delayed because the position has been vacant since Sept 24, 2026, the bank said. The bank has also assigned a moderate-to-substantial risk rating to the $70m Connected Punjab Programme for political, governance, macroeconomic, and fiduciary reasons, effective from the start of the current fiscal year and running until June 2031. This is despite the bank conceding that the programme benefited from “strong ownership at the highest levels of the Government of Punjab”. The programme focuses on three mutually reinforcing results areas: broadband access and connectivity; digital service delivery and artificial intelligence (AI) readiness; and enhanced cashless transactions. The Punjab Information Technology Board (PITB) has secured provincial government approval, demonstrating strong institutional preparedness. Next steps include advancing the AI Oversight Committee, Data Governance Framework, personal data protection strategy, and cybersecurity strategy as foundations for responsible AI adoption. The PRID-MPA was approved by the WB board of directors on Dec 19, 2025, while describing it as an innovative, national programme supporting federal and provincial reforms to mobilise domestic revenue and enhance spending quality and leverage data and digital tools for improved services. Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

items.title: Dessalement, énergie, industrie : les filières marocaines en quête de synergies
items.description: Réunis du 25 au 28 novembre à Casablanca, elec expo, EneR Event et Tronica Expo mettront en relation les acteurs de l’électricité, des énergies renouvelables et des technologies industrielles. Au programme : les infrastructures stratégiques, le dessalement et les possibilités de coopération industrielle, avec l’Italie comme pays à l’honneur. Le développement des infrastructures hydriques et énergétiques ouvre un champ de débouchés aux industriels marocains, à mesure que les besoins en eau, en électricité et en équipements technologiques prennent une place croissante dans les projets d’investissement. C’est autour de cette articulation entre souveraineté industrielle et grands chantiers nationaux que s’organisera la prochaine édition des salons elec expo, EneR Event et Tronica Expo, prévue du 25 au 28 novembre 2026 à la Foire Internationale de Casablanca. Placée sous le Haut Patronage du Roi Mohammed VI, cette manifestation réunira des professionnels marocains et internationaux issus de plus de 30 pays. Organisée par la Fédération Nationale de l’Électricité, de l’Électronique et des Énergies Renouvelables (FENELEC), avec Global Fairs & Events comme organisateur délégué, elle aura pour thème « Vision 2030 : Infrastructures stratégiques & dessalement au service de la souveraineté industrielle ». Au-delà de la présentation de technologies et d’équipements, le rendez-vous entend rapprocher les entreprises des différentes filières qui interviennent dans la conception, la réalisation et l’exploitation des infrastructures. L’objectif est de favoriser les échanges commerciaux, le transfert de technologies et l’émergence de partenariats susceptibles d’accompagner les investissements nationaux, tout en renforçant les capacités productives locales. Le dessalement, un marché transversal pour l’industrie Le choix de placer le dessalement au centre des débats souligne la convergence entre les enjeux hydriques, énergétiques et industriels. Une station de dessalement ne repose pas uniquement sur des installations de traitement de l’eau. Son fonctionnement mobilise également des équipements électriques, des systèmes de contrôle et d’instrumentation, des solutions d’automatisation, des dispositifs de maintenance ainsi que, potentiellement, l’intégration de sources d’énergie renouvelable. La performance de ces installations dépend notamment de la fiabilité des équipements, de l’optimisation de leur consommation énergétique et de la maîtrise du coût de l’eau produite. Autant de paramètres qui font intervenir des compétences complémentaires, depuis l’électrotechnique jusqu’à l’électronique industrielle, en passant par les technologies de pilotage et l’efficacité énergétique. Cette interdépendance donne aux entreprises spécialisées dans ces domaines des perspectives de positionnement sur les marchés liés aux infrastructures hydriques. Elle met également en évidence l’intérêt d’une intégration industrielle locale, permettant de valoriser les savoir-faire nationaux dans la fourniture d’équipements, l’ingénierie et les services techniques. À l’horizon 2030, la disponibilité de l’électricité, la fiabilité des installations et l’accès à l’eau figurent parmi les conditions nécessaires pour accompagner les investissements et le développement industriel. Les salons entendent ainsi contribuer à rapprocher les fournisseurs de solutions technologiques des industriels, des bureaux d’études, des investisseurs et des porteurs de projets. Cette orientation s’inscrit dans le prolongement des Hautes Directives royales relatives à l’accélération des projets d’infrastructures et au lancement d’une nouvelle génération de stratégies dans les domaines de la sécurité hydrique et énergétique, de l’industrie, de l’économie numérique et de l’intelligence artificielle. Dans Son discours du 9 octobre 2026, à l’occasion de l’ouverture de la première session de la première année législative de la douzième législature, le Souverain a également appelé le secteur privé national à renforcer son rôle dans la transformation économique du pays, notamment par l’investissement, l’innovation, la création d’emplois et le développement des exportations. Trois salons pour rapprocher les filières La tenue simultanée des trois manifestations doit permettre de croiser des expertises qui interviennent souvent sur les mêmes projets, mais relèvent de spécialités distinctes. Dans sa 19e édition, elec expo réunira les acteurs de l’électricité, de l’éclairage, de l’électrotechnique et de l’automatisation industrielle. Les solutions présentées porteront notamment sur la modernisation des infrastructures et l’amélioration de la sécurité et de la fiabilité des installations. La 14e édition d’EneR Event sera consacrée aux énergies renouvelables et à l’efficacité énergétique. Elle mettra en avant les technologies liées à la diversification des sources d’énergie, à la maîtrise des consommations et à la décarbonation de l’économie. De son côté, Tronica Expo, qui tiendra sa 13e édition, couvrira l’électronique, la sécurité électronique, le bâtiment intelligent, l’avionique, la mécatronique et l’aéronautique. Une place particulière sera accordée aux systèmes intelligents et à la transformation technologique. La complémentarité de ces trois univers constitue l’un des principaux axes de la manifestation. Les besoins des infrastructures énergétiques et hydriques dépassent en effet la seule fourniture d’équipements : ils impliquent aussi des solutions de supervision, de contrôle, d’automatisation et de maintenance, ainsi que des compétences capables d’en assurer l’intégration. Pour les entreprises marocaines, l’enjeu consiste à tirer parti de ces interactions afin de développer leurs activités, d’améliorer leurs compétences et d’accéder à de nouveaux marchés, notamment en Afrique. L’Italie, partenaire industriel à l’honneur La dimension internationale sera marquée par la participation de l’Italie en qualité de pays à l’honneur. L’Agence italienne pour le commerce extérieur (ICE) organisera un pavillon national réunissant des entreprises actives dans les énergies renouvelables, l’électronique et l’électrotechnique. Cette présence doit favoriser les échanges entre opérateurs marocains et italiens, le partage d’expertise et la formation de partenariats industriels. Elle ouvre également des perspectives de coopération sur les marchés africains, où les besoins en infrastructures, en équipements et en solutions énergétiques offrent des possibilités de développement aux entreprises des deux pays. Le programme prévoit, pendant les quatre jours de la manifestation, des conférences consacrées aux enjeux stratégiques, des présentations technologiques et des rencontres d’affaires B2B. Industriels, bureaux d’études, prescripteurs, décideurs publics et porteurs de projets y seront réunis, avec la participation d’acteurs marocains et internationaux, notamment d’Afrique subsaharienne. À travers cette édition conjointe, la FENELEC entend mobiliser la complémentarité des filières électriques, énergétiques et technologiques au service des grands projets du Royaume. Pour les entreprises, les retombées attendues se situent autant dans les opportunités commerciales immédiates que dans la consolidation de partenariats, la montée en compétences et le développement de capacités industrielles locales. The post Dessalement, énergie, industrie : les filières marocaines en quête de synergies appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Israeli settlers set fire to mosque in occupied West Bank
items.description: MIKHMAS: Israeli settlers set fire to a mosque and graffitied its outside walls on Wednesday in the occupied West Bank village of Mikhmas, Palestinian sources and the Israeli military said. Atta Kanaan, a Palestinian resident of Mikhmas who lives 50 metres from the mosque, told AFP that he heard the sound of breaking glass shortly after midnight on Wednesday and immediately went to the building. “A fire was burning fiercely, and we called the fire brigade. Young men rushed to help us with fire extinguishers, and we managed to contain part of the fire before the flames engulfed the entire mosque,” he said. Israel’s military told AFP that soldiers were dispatched to Mikhmas following a report of graffiti and arson at the mosque, as well as damage to a vehicle. “No suspects were identified,” it said, adding an investigation had been opened. AFP video footage showed that the fire had burned down the mosque’s interior carpeting and blackened the walls. An AFP journalist reported that slogans were spraypainted in Hebrew on the exterior walls, including “just because we are quiet doesn’t mean we are asleep”. Settlers also set fire to a car, Kanaan said, adding that in recent weeks villagers had formed night-watch patrols out of fear that settlers might torch homes, particularly those on the outskirts of the village. Rouhi Fattouh, president of the Palestinian National Council, described the arson attack on the mosque as “a barbaric act and a dangerous escalation in settler terrorism”. Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

items.title: Drop-off charges at UK airports to be reviewed after sharp increase
items.description: Airport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years. Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges the most expensive, jumping from £7 to £10. Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from £6 to £8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from £5 to £8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City. The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was “vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly”. The government added it hoped airports would “exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives”. ‘Rip-off’ The RAC, which conducted the analysis in July this year, has campaigned against increases in drop-off charges. It said a review of “kiss and fly” fees would be “music to the ears of drivers”. “We know airport drop-off charges are a growing source of anger and frustration,” said Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC. “Four-in-five drivers we’ve surveyed believe they are a ‘rip-off’, with just one-in-10 understanding why airports charge what they do.” The RAC’s research found London City Airport, which only introduced charges in 2026, was the most expensive on a per-minute basis. Its £8 charge for five minutes works out at £1.60 per minute. Belfast International Airport now charges £5 for 10 minutes in the drop-off zone, up £2 on last year. None of the top 10 airports in the European Union charge for drop-offs, according to the RAC. It argues that international airports should not charge for passenger drop-offs; however, the industry said such charges are a necessary part of airports’ business models. Supporters of such charges also say they encourage travellers to use more environmentally friendly modes of transport. “Airports outside the UK are typically publicly owned and in receipt of state subsidies and tax exemptions, while UK airports are generally privately owned and subject to the full array of commercial rates of taxation,” said Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, which represents airports. She added airports offered a “range of options for those travelling to terminals, including free drop-off points” and that “any review” by the government would find airports make “excellent use of a variety of ways to manage traffic and air pollution”. The Aviation Environment Federation campaign group has previously defended the fees, arguing they help reduce congestion and air pollution around airports. Earlier this month, the government announced extra charges for parents sitting with their children when flying would be scrapped in time for next year’s summer holidays. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the changes were part of a series of “everyday fixes” to ease cost-of-living pressures on households.

items.title: Kenya confirms second Ebola case – a relative of the first victim
items.description: Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola, 10 days after a businessman died of the virus after he had travelled to the East African nation from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The new patient, a 39-year-old man, is a close relative of the first case and was already in quarantine when he fell ill on Tuesday, Kenya’s health ministry says. The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. Detecting his illness early had improved his chances of recovery and limited the chance of him passing the virus on to others, the ministry said, as it urged the public to “stay calm but vigilant”. “Both cases are linked, and there is no evidence of spread in the wider community,” the ministry said. “Kenya remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings”, it added. The 40-year-old Kenyan man who died on 5 October was diagnosed with Ebola shortly after being admitted to hospital in the capital, Nairobi. A relative had taken him there shortly after picking him up at the airport. He had travelled from DR Congo, through Uganda to Kenya without his illness being detected. Since his death, officials had determined that he had been in contact with 128 people – and since Tuesday 113 of them had been found, the health ministry said. Of these, 108 were in quarantine in Kenya and tracing of the remaining 15 continued, it said. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. “Anyone with fever, unusual tiredness, muscle or joint pains, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding should seek care promptly at the nearest health facility,” Kenya’s health ministry said. The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment – though trials are under way. Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died. However, the World Health Organisation (WHO) declared that the country was free of the disease in August. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the continent’s leading public health agency, has reconstructed the Kenyan patient’s movements for the six weeks leading up to his death. It revealed that he first started feeling unwell in DR Congo on 15 September – and showed how several opportunities to detect the infection were missed, including during several visits to Congolese medical facilities. He then managed to travel through Uganda to Kenya – and was again not detected at airport screenings. Health experts say it highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.

items.title: Hidden video recording device found in cabin of Australian navy ship
items.description: A hidden video recording device has been found in an Australian navy ship’s cabin, the Australian Defence Force (ADF) has confirmed. The device was located on Sunday in the cabin of Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin in Cairns, Queensland. The confirmation came after independent Australian senator Jacqui Lambie, a former veteran and defence advocate, told parliament she was contacted by personnel with allegations that “concealed cameras have recently been found in the female sailors’ showers facilities”. Australia’s defence department has not said whether the device was found in a female-only space and said the incident was referred to the Joint Military Police United. Lambie told the Australian Senate on Wednesday: “I was also told this had occurred recently and prevented the vessel from sailing while investigations were ongoing. Even more disturbing are claims that footage from these cameras may have been uploaded online before the cameras were discovered. “How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask navy.” Later on Wednesday, the defence department confirmed it became aware of a video recording device being found in a HMAS Leeuwin cabin but did not give specific details on where it was discovered. “Defence takes this incident extremely seriously and does not tolerate unacceptable behaviour in any form,” the department said in its statement. “The ship remained alongside to enable the investigation and ensure immediate support was provided to members of the ship’s crew. The welfare of individuals remains Defence’s priority, and support is ongoing. “As the matter is currently under investigation and to protect the privacy of the affected individuals, Defence is unable to provide further comment at this time.”

items.title: Lawmakers, govt differ over Discos’ privatisation
items.description: • Muhammad Ali claims CCI nod not required, says Discos caused over $30bn in losses over 15 years • Panel seeks records of council’s decisions, other consultations • Questions Rs2.6tr federal spending on devolved subjects ISLAMABAD: The propo­sed privatisation of power distribution companies (Discos) stirred controversy on Wedn­esday, as a Senate panel maintained that the matter constitutionally fell within the domain of the Council of Common Interests (CCI), while the government’s top privatisation official insisted that no fresh CCI approval was required. Adviser to the Prime Minister on Privatisation Muhammad Ali told a subcommittee of the Senate Functional Committee on Devolution that no new CCI approval was needed for the privatisation of Discos. He added that the companies had caused losses of more than $30 billion over the past 15 years. He said the CCI had approved the privatisation of three power generation companies and nine distribution companies in 2011. It also approved the National Electricity Policy on June 21, 2021, which recommended that the government explore various privatisation options to improve the efficiency of state-owned entities where applicable. Both decisions remained valid, he said. On the validity of the decisions, the law division, in a Sept 25, 2026 letter, reconfirmed that in light of the 2011 CCI decision, fresh approval was not required for the privatisation of Discos. Accordingly, the privatisation division maintained that no fresh CCI approval was required in light of the 2011 decision and the 2021 National Electricity Policy, Mr Ali said. The adviser told the subcommittee that legal and procedural requirements for the privatisation process had been fulfilled. He said the National Electricity Policy 2021 had been formulated after obtaining recommendations from the provinces and that the privatisation programme had subsequently been approved, with further work undertaken during 2023-24. Referring the matter back to the CCI at this stage could cause significant delays, affect investor confidence and adversely impact the financial position of power distribution companies, he argued. Highlighting substantial losses faced by the power sector due to electricity theft and operational inefficiencies, he stressed that privatisation was necessary to improve performance and reduce burden on the national exchequer. Responding, subcommittee convener Senator Zamir Hussain Ghumro emphasised that the constitutional position and role of the CCI could not be overlooked. He questioned whether the proposed privatisation was consistent with the constitutional distribution of powers under Article 157, observing that electricity distribution and related matters involved provincial interests. Referring to previous judicial decisions and privatisation initiatives, he stressed the importance of transparency and protecting provincial interests, and asked authorities to provide relevant decisions and supporting documents for examination. He said provinces, being represented in the CCI, should have an opportunity to consider matters falling within their domain. Officials informed the committee that the CCI had taken 11 relevant decisions and that, according to available record, no province had formally recorded reservations. They assured that relevant documents and details of provincial consultations would be shared. The minister reiterated that all necessary legal requirements had been met and referring the matter back to CCI was not considered necessary at this stage. The chairman reiterated that the committee’s examination was intended to ensure constitutional compliance, transparency and effective parliamentary oversight, and directed authorities to furnish decisions and supporting documents so the matter could be assessed in light of the Constitution and previous judicial pronouncements. He said constitutionally the matter was related to CCI and necessary documents must be submitted to examine the process from all aspects. The subcommittee met under the convenorship of Senator Ghumro to review federal expenditure on ministries, institutions, organisations, statutory bodies and corporations retained by the federal government despite provincial matters following the 18th Constitutional Amendment. It also examined compliance reports and status of matters concerning the CCI. The meeting was attended by Senators Jan Muhammad Buledi and Poonjo Bheel, secretaries of cabinet, CCI, Establishment Division, special secretary establishment, additional secretary establishment and senior officers. At the outset, the report of the Auditor General of Pakistan (AGP) and the Accountant General on expenditure incurred by the federal government on ministries relating to provincial subjects was taken up. The chairman observed that despite 16 years since the 18th Amendment, concerns persisted regarding federal expenditure on devolved subjects, including education and health, which had been notified as provincial matters by the Implementation Commission. Referring to Articles 168 and 169 of the Constitution and the legal framework governing the audit of public expenditure, he questioned the authorisation and constitutional basis for expenditure of approximately Rs2.6 trillion on the health and education ministries over the past 16 years. He termed the expenditure of Rs2.6tr by the federal government on the two ministries, which he said had been de-notified in 2010, a misuse of taxpayers’ money, arguing that the Centre could spend only on federal subjects. He said the amount could rise to several trillion rupees once expenditure on other ministries created for provincial subjects was included. Mr Ghumro expressed concern that the details sought by the committee had not been submitted within the stipulated timeframe and stressed that parliament was the primary authority for authorising public expenditure, and that such expenditure should be confined to federal subjects. He maintained that expenditure from the Federal Consolidated Fund could not be authorised for devolved provincial matters. AGP officials explained that the audit process was guided by budgets approved by the competent parliamentary forum and acknowledged certain limitations in coverage. Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

items.title: Saudi Arabia overturns death sentence for man over Facebook comment, Sri Lanka says
items.description: Saudi Arabia’s Supreme Court has set aside the death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan migrant worker over a comment he made on Facebook, Colombo’s Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra said. Anojan Sivarasa, 27, was sentenced to death in September after a Saudi appellate court convicted him of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over his comment. The case sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka , spurring diplomatic efforts to seek clemency. Saudi Arabia’s top court set aside the sentence on Wednesday, Hemachandra said in a Facebook post, thanking the authorities and legal teams of both nations for their efforts. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online. During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Sivarasa to respond in Tamil, insulting the Prophet Muhammad. Although Sivarasa promptly deleted the comment and posted an apology video, a screenshot of it was brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July. It is not clear if there will be further legal proceedings or whether Sivarasa will remain in detention, and for how long. He was initially sentenced to five years in prison and a fine of three million Saudi riyals ($0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. Faizer Mustafa, a Sri Lankan lawmaker who is involved in legal negotiations with Saudi Arabia regarding Sivarasa’s case, confirmed to BBC Sinhala that Saudi Arabia had overturned the death sentence, adding that they are reviewing the Supreme Court’s latest ruling. Sivarasa’s family had earlier said they have had no direct contact with him since 28 September. International rights groups had also joined calls for Saudi to spare his life. “Saudi authorities should end their use of abusive laws to hand out extraordinary sentences for speech-related offences, especially against migrant workers who are already in a vulnerable position with limited protections,” Joey Shea, a senior Saudi Arabia researcher at Human Rights Watch, said on Tuesday.

items.title: China calls for end to political deadlock in Libya
items.description: A Chinese envoy to the UN on Wednesday called for efforts to break the political deadlock in Libya as soon as possible. The agreement reached through the UN-facilitated "4+4" smaller convening marked important progress in implementing the political roadmap in Libya. China hopes that the agreement will help unify Libya's state institutions and lay the foundation for national elections and the completion of the political transition, said Sun Lei, China's deputy permanent representative to the United Nations. At the same time, he said, whether the agreement can be truly implemented depends on whether it can gain broad support from all Libyan parties. In supporting Libya's political process, the international community must uphold the Libyan-led and Libyan-owned principle and avoid imposing external solutions. The political deadlock must be broken as soon as possible, he told the Security Council. "Libya's security situation is closely linked to its political process. Any new armed conflict could undermine hard-won mutual trust and render political efforts futile," he said. Recently, attacks on energy facilities have continued in western Libya, and the resulting tensions are a cause for concern. The parties concerned should stop the attacks and refrain from taking any action that could lead to a deterioration of the situation, Sun said. The unification of military and security institutions is crucial to maintaining a lasting ceasefire and is also an important condition for ensuring the smooth conduct of elections and the transfer of power. China supports the eastern and western sides in strengthening dialogue, building mutual trust, and accelerating the process, he said. The international community, on the basis of respecting Libya's sovereignty and ownership, should provide greater support to the country in strengthening border management, combating transnational criminal networks, and curbing the illicit flow of weapons, he added. Sun also called for efforts to improve economic governance and people's livelihoods in Libya. The international community should call on all Libyan parties to fully implement the unified budget framework, strengthen fiscal transparency and independent oversight, and make greater efforts to support Libya in combating oil smuggling, to ensure that its oil revenues are used for national development and the well-being of its people. International partners should support Libyan authorities in improving public services and advancing development and reconstruction, to strengthen public confidence in national unity, stability and development, he said. As a good friend of Libya, China stands ready to continue working with all parties and make greater efforts to help Libya achieve lasting peace and stability and enable its people to live and work in peace and contentment at an early date, Sun said.

items.title: Burnham says he wants to ‘repair bridges’ between Ukraine and US
items.description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will try to “repair bridges” between Ukraine and the United States, ahead of a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street. The Ukrainian president was welcomed by a military ceremonial guard outside Number 10 upon his arrival for the meeting, in what is thought to be a first for a foreign leader. It comes after President Donald Trump said he had struck a deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel. Asked about Trump’s move during Prime Minister’s Questions, Burnham resisted criticising the US president, saying he wanted to “be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together”. However, he stressed that Zelensky would not be leaving the UK “empty-handed”, adding that further military and financial support would be arranged in the coming weeks. Burnham is expected to use the visit to promise further sanctions against Russia, while also announcing the UK will accelerate its delivery of air defence missiles to Kyiv. The UK will also urge allies to step up pressure on Russia, with Chancellor John Healey using International Monetary Fund meetings to call for a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG). It is Zelensky’s second visit to the UK since Burnham became prime minister. While other world leaders have received military welcomes, Number 10 said it could not find a record of one taking place on Downing Street. The King held an audience with President Zelensky at Buckingham Palace as part of his visit to the UK During PMQs, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey asked whether he agreed the diesel deal was “yet another shameful Trump betrayal of the Ukrainian people and European security”. In response, Burnham did not echo Sir Ed’s condemnation of Trump, saying: “What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back and therefore I should at this moment in time be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together.” The PM said he had spoken to Zelensky over the phone on Saturday “because I recognised it was another very dark and difficult moment for him as they contemplate a winter that will be severe for his people”. The phone call came after Trump announced that President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US, as he suspended sanctions on diesel from Moscow. Zelensky branded the move a gift to Putin, warning it would provide Moscow with money to continue its war against Ukraine. Trump responded by saying it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” . Meanwhile, Zelensky has said at least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes . He said “critical” energy infrastructure had been hit – despite Trump’s claim on Sunday that a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure was in place between Russia and Ukraine. Russia said its strikes had hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine’s military. Zelensky has said Ukraine is ready to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow did the same. But Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said Ukraine does not deserve the “respite” a ceasefire would bring.

items.title: Pope walking and recovering ‘as expected’ after surgery, doctors say
items.description: Pope Leo XIV’s recovery from surgery to remove a lower lobe of his lung is “progressing as expected”, his doctors have said. The 71-year-old pontiff has started to walk and has “resumed a normal diet” following the roughly 90-minute procedure, the medics said in an update shared by the Vatican. The Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been “successful” and proceeded without complications. Blood tests and an X-ray early on Wednesday showed his recovery was “proceeding normally”, the doctors said, and he has also undergone respiratory physiotherapy. The whole lower lobe of the Pope’s right lung was removed “to ensure the procedure was radical”, the Vatican said following the surgery. “After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room,” it said earlier, before spending a “peaceful night” at the hospital. The pontiff is expected to remain there for about a week as he recovers. He had announced that he would be admitted for the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter’s Square that doctors had found a “well-contained” nodule on his lung “at an early stage” and advised him to have it removed. Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, “as suspected by pre-operative tests”, the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma. A Vatican source told news agency AFP that further tests were carried out to see whether the cancer had spread. The Vatican has stressed that the Pope, who is generally considered fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness. The news has shaken Catholics worldwide, many of whom will have recent memories of Pope Francis’s hospital visits. Pope Leo’s predecessor, who died last year, also had part of his lung removed in his youth before suffering a series of respiratory infections later in life. What is lung adenocarcinoma? Adenocarcinomas develop in cells that produce mucus and are one of the most common types of lung cancer. The long-term prognosis depends on a number of things, including the stage of the cancer when identified and the person’s overall health. The earlier it is spotted, the better, and treatments have improved over the last few decades. Some adenocarcinomas are picked up early – before symptoms develop – during routine tests. At later stages, lung cancer can cause a persistent cough, breathlessness, fatigue and weight loss.

items.title: Pakistan worst hit by hunger in South Asia
items.description: • Economic instability erodes household purchasing power; heavy rains, floods trigger acute crop losses • ​South Asia remains in the ‘serious’ category; ​global hunger rises after two decades ISLAMABAD: Pakistan recorded the highest score in South Asia on the 2026 Global Hunger Index released on Wednesday, reflecting a worsening food security crisis driven by economic instability, climate shocks and global conflicts. Published jointly by Welthungerhilfe, the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict at Ruhr University Bochum, and the Swiss organisation Helvetas under the theme “No Security Without Food Security”, the report reveals that progress in South Asia has largely stagnated, with conditions in Pakistan and Afghanistan deteriorating since 2018. In Pakistan, economic instability and sharp food price inflation have eroded households’ purchasing power and constrained access to food. Undernourishment in the country has climbed from low in 2018 to medium, while child wasting has risen toward the high threshold. Across South Asia, the situation remains serious with a regional score of 23.5. Although the region’s score has fallen substantially from an alarming 37.5 in 2000, most of that progress occurred before 2018. While Pakistan and Afghanistan have moved from the alarming to the serious category since 2000, child stunting remains very high. Pakistan’s stunting rate continues to fall, whereas Afghanistan’s has edged up since 2018. Child mortality rates in both nations have declined from very high levels in 2000 to medium levels today. The report warned that high levels of acute food insecurity will persist across the region. Heavy rains and flooding caused localised crop losses in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh, while below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures negatively affected Afghanistan’s 2026 cereal-growing season. According to Food and Agriculture Organisation estimates, 218 million people in South Asia, including Iran, were undernourished between 2023 and 2025, representing roughly one-third of the global total. Globally, hunger is rising again after nearly two decades of progress. The 2026 global score stands at 18.1, worsening from 17.6 in 2018. Hunger has increased in 32 countries since 2018, and 57 countries are on track to miss achieving even low hunger levels by 2030. Three of the index’s four indicators — undernourishment, child stunting and child wasting — have worsened, while only child mortality has continued to decline slightly. State-based armed conflicts, now at their highest level since World War II, alongside frequent extreme weather events, are major drivers of this reversal. The war in Iran and shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait are driving up fuel, transportation and fertiliser costs. Meanwhile, Russia’s war in Ukraine and Black Sea export restrictions threaten higher wheat prices, making basic supplies unaffordable in the Global South. Compounding the crisis, international spending on food security has fallen to 2016-2017 levels, forcing cuts to aid programmes and emergency rations. The report urged governments to reverse funding cuts for humanitarian assistance and data collection to prevent and manage future crises. Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

items.title: 10 Ghanaian institutions receive GH¢7m Canadian grant to train scholars, restore degraded environments
items.description: Ten Ghanaian public and private sector institutions are accessing a GH¢7 million foreign grant to strengthen technical expertise to tackle environmental degradation and empower women along the forest value chain. The five-year partnership with Lakehead University in Canada will involve training 36 Ghanaians in wood science and technology, remote sensing and geomatics, ecological remediation, and forestry. The goal is to open more local avenues for promoting sustainable natural resource management. The public universities benefiting from the partnership include the University of Ghana, KNUST, Cape Coast University, UDS, the University of Energy and Natural Resources (UENR), and the CSIR College of Science and Technology. Other beneficiary institutions are the Forestry Commission, the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research’s FORIG, Samartex Timber and Plywood Company, and the Charcoal Chamber of Commerce – Ghana. The funding regime, which is part of the Global Affairs Canada Bachelor of Computer Science and Digital Innovation (BCDI) project, will enable 26 countries across Africa to access an $80 million program. He is optimistic Ghana could still benefit more from the Canadian government. “The Global Affairs Canada BCDI project is an eight-year program that has $80 million in funding across all of the different projects, and there are 26 nations in Africa that are part of this program. I’m bringing about GH¢7m to Ghana on this one grant. This is not the only one we’re going to get, trust me”. Professor Matthew Leitch of the Faculty of Natural Resources Management at Lakehead University revealed. Prof Matthew Leitch Professor Matthew Leitch of the Faculty of Natural Resources Management at Lakehead University detailed the initiative during a media engagement in Kumasi. He says the new era highlights a relationship dating back to 1992 with the Canadian Economic Development Agency. “The idea is to train lots of people and hopefully uh improve the lives of all Ghanaians and the environment here. We have seen some of the main areas of the UN strategies, and, after initial meetings, areas they found we could benefit from. “So things like the illegal mining, using some of our remote sensing technologies combined with forestry and wood science or more forestry as far as replanting and so reclamation, remediation and afforestation.” According to him, the partnership involves leveraging advanced Canadian technologies to address several environmental challenges faced by Ghana, including illegal mining and deforestation. “Future remote sensing and geomatics training programs will be structured around specific needs and issues in Ghana, with an upcoming one-month training session planned for approximately eight participants from various institutions. “This initiative forms part of broader efforts that include senior-level executives to ensure knowledge is applied effectively from the top down.” The partnership provides full scholarships to three Master’s students at Lakehead University and sponsorship for 23 early to mid-career officers through tailored certificate programs Professor Mrs Mercy Afua Adutwumwaa Derkyi is the Former Dean of the School of Natural Resources at the University of Energy and Natural Resources(UENR). “You know, this program is beneficial in terms of our capacity building. Building our capacity in knowledge, in skills, and also networking and strengthening our partnership,” she told the media. For the Forestry Commission, the partnership comes at a time when forest reserves and resources are under attack from illegal activities. Authorities are hopeful that the introduction of modern approaches, such as remote sensing and mapping, to combat illegalities will yield positive results, as some of the Commission’s staff undergo training in Canada. Valerie Fumey Nassah is the Director of Operations Plantations at the Forestry Commission. “The project is also very useful for us because we are at a critical time in the history of this country when all our forest reserves, all our forest reserves and forest resources in general are under attack from illegal activities. “We have illegal mining, we have illegal farming, we have people putting up settlements in our forest reserves, which are only 15% of the entire country. So if we are able to monitor in real time, we will be able to ensure that we reduce the degradation and deforestation of our reserves.” Madam Nassah is elated by the program’s uniqueness. “One unique thing about this BCDI 2030 project is that for all the participants in the training, 51% will have to be women. And it is not normal. It does not always happen like that, so we are very happy. “It’s not only about gender, but ensuring that the small percentage of females who are in the forestry sector get the opportunity to upgrade their skills, get knowledge, and expertise to be able to manage our resources just like our male counterparts are doing.” A private timber company, Samatex, wants to use the opportunity presented by the partnership to conduct further studies on the behavior of lesser-known timber species and develop them into viable sought-after. Justice Eshun, the head of the Forestry Department at Samartex, says the company will take advantage of the partnership to research tree species “As a company, we are always looking to develop the lesser-used species. I believe we don’t know much about “Esa”; we don’t know much about “Esiaa”, and we don’t even use it much. “So what we are doing as a company with this project is that they are advanced. We are looking at lesser-used species. When we say “lesser-used species,” we mean species that are not common on the market and that people are not using. “What we are looking at now is that we are doing research with Lakehead University, and we are trying to see how trees behave differently across landscapes. We are saying this because very soon the trees that we know, the trees that we know so much, the Mahoganies and when you go there, you’re not going to find them anymore.” At least 51 per cent of all scholarship recipients under the BCDI 2030 partnership are women, as it seeks to develop those who can serve as change agents.
